subject: DTF/DIF in quasi-experimental design: What to do with items with DIF?

messages.author: eab9582ba50c948a
messages.subject: DTF/DIF in quasi-experimental design: What to do with items with DIF?
parts:
Hi everyone,

I’m writing here because I’ve been struggling to find good literature on DIF/DTF analysis in controlled experiments, and I’m hoping you can help.

For my PhD, I’m using a quasi-experimental design with two intervention groups and one control group. I’m measuring (mathematical) abilities at three points: Pre, Post, and Follow-Up, using the same 11-item test for all groups and time points, analyzed with a unidimensional graded response model (GRM).

To make sure I can confidently use the scale across groups and time points (and later run regression analyses), I decided to check for measurement invariance. The way I see it, I only need to compare two groups:
1. Students with no instruction in the subject (all groups at Pretest and the control group at all time points).
2. Students who’ve received instruction (Post and Follow-Up for the intervention groups).

I ran DIF and DTF (DRF) analyses for these two groups (all in all N=710) and found three items with DIF, as well as significant unsigned DRF (but not significant signed DRF). Results are included below.

Now, I’m unsure about two things:
1. Does my approach to grouping and running the analyses make sense?
2. What should I do with the items showing DIF?

I’m not keen on dropping them. Should I try a model with group-specific GRM parameters (as suggested by Liu & Rogers, 2022, DOI: 10.1177/00131644211012050)? Or would it be okay to assume the DTF reflects something inherent to students who have or haven’t had instruction and thus just ignore it?

I’d really appreciate your thoughts and advice!

Thanks a lot

Martin

messages.subject: Re: DTF/DIF in quasi-experimental design: What to do with items with DIF?
parts:
Hi Martin,

Your approach sounds reasonable to me. However, I do wonder how you went about managing the time factor in this design as technically each time point reflects some type of potential change in the individuals (even the in the control group, whose traits may be influenced by regression to the mean effects). I would think of this design as one where you have three highly correlated traits due to the three measurement occasions, where by construction the items are treated invariant over time (at least initially) while the traits are allowed to have different means/variances per group. Once the scaling effects over time are taken into account in the model then you can move into the DIF testing flavour by removing one or more item parameter constraints over the measurement occasions. 

Of course, you can focus on one point at a time as well, which would also get at the idea of measurement invariance within each occasion, though I would worry about family-wise error control as that's a lot of testing .... HTH for now.

For my PhD, I’m using a quasi-experimental design with two intervention groups and one control group. I’m measuring (mathematical) abilities at three points: Pre, Post, and Follow-Up, using the same 11-item test for all groups and time points, analyzed with a unidimensional graded response model (GRM).

To make sure I can confidently use the scale across groups and time points (and later run regression analyses), I decided to check for measurement invariance. The way I see it, I only need to compare two groups:
1. Students with no instruction in the subject (all groups at Pretest and the control group at all time points).
2. Students who’ve received instruction (Post and Follow-Up for the intervention groups).

I ran DIF and DTF (DRF) analyses for these two groups (all in all N=710) and found three items with DIF, as well as significant unsigned DRF (but not significant signed DRF). Results are included below.

Now, I’m unsure about two things:
1. Does my approach to grouping and running the analyses make sense?
2. What should I do with the items showing DIF?

I’m not keen on dropping them. Should I try a model with group-specific GRM parameters (as suggested by Liu & Rogers, 2022, DOI: 10.1177/00131644211012050)? Or would it be okay to assume the DTF reflects something inherent to students who have or haven’t had instruction and thus just ignore it?

I’d really appreciate your thoughts and advice!

Thanks a lot

Martin

parts:
Me again, sorry. I've had the idea to let ChatGPT explain to me, what you meant by including the scaling effects, and this (generic) code is basically the summary of his answers. It reads logically but never trust a machine, so maybe you could have a quick assessment of it? Thanks, Martin

# Define the model: Three latent traits (one for each time point: Pretest, Posttest, Follow-Up)
model <- '
  Trait1 = 1-11  # Pretest
  Trait2 = 1-11  # Posttest
  Trait3 = 1-11  # Follow-Up
  COV = Trait1*Trait2*Trait3  # Allow correlations between traits
'

# Step 1: Fit the initial model assuming measurement invariance
# (All items are treated as invariant across groups and time points)
model_invariant <- multipleGroup(
  data,                # Dataset containing item responses
  model,               # Model structure with three latent traits
  group = Grpvect,     # Grouping variable (e.g., intervention vs. control group)
  itemtype = 'graded', # Graded response model for polytomous items
  invariance = c("slopes", "intercepts")  # Fix slopes and intercepts across groups
)
summary(model_invariant)

# Step 2: Check scaling effects
# Extract group-specific means and variances for the three latent traits
scaling_effects <- coef(model_invariant, simplify = TRUE)$GroupPars
print(scaling_effects)
# Interpretation: Differences in means (MEAN_1, MEAN_2, MEAN_3) or variances (VAR_1, VAR_2, VAR_3)
# indicate potential group or time-point effects.

# Step 3: Relax the invariance for specific items flagged for DIF
# (Based on prior DIF analysis, allow parameters for W_5C, W_6A, and W_9A to vary)
model_DIF <- multipleGroup(
  data,                # Dataset containing item responses
  model,               # Model structure with three latent traits
  group = Grpvect,     # Grouping variable
  itemtype = 'graded', # Graded response model for polytomous items
  invariance = c(
    "slopes", "intercepts",     # General invariance for most items
    "W_5C", "W_6A", "W_9A"      # Allow these items to vary across groups (DIF testing)
  )
)
summary(model_DIF)

# Step 4: Conduct DIF and DTF analyses
# Evaluate item-level DIF and overall test-level bias
DRF_results <- DRF(
  model_DIF,         # Updated model with relaxed invariance
  draws = 1000,      # Number of Monte Carlo draws for confidence intervals
  DIF = TRUE,        # Include DIF testing
  p.adjust = "BH"    # Adjust p-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg method
)

Hey Phil, 

thanks for your answer, it’s really great to receive your direct feedback on my question!

The theoretical idea of my approach is to build the two groups as described to NOT have to worry about any time factor. I simply assume that students without instruction are «kind of the same» independent of whenever they pass the test and the same for students WITH instruction, disregarding any time points. Do you think, that’s too much of a simplification of the reality? If yes, how would you measure the scaling effects you wrote about and add them to the model?

Thank you very much, Martin

Am 17.01.2025 um 21:43 schrieb Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com>:

Hi Martin,

Your approach sounds reasonable to me. However, I do wonder how you went about managing the time factor in this design as technically each time point reflects some type of potential change in the individuals (even the in the control group, whose traits may be influenced by regression to the mean effects). I would think of this design as one where you have three highly correlated traits due to the three measurement occasions, where by construction the items are treated invariant over time (at least initially) while the traits are allowed to have different means/variances per group. Once the scaling effects over time are taken into account in the model then you can move into the DIF testing flavour by removing one or more item parameter constraints over the measurement occasions. 

Of course, you can focus on one point at a time as well, which would also get at the idea of measurement invariance within each occasion, though I would worry about family-wise error control as that's a lot of testing .... HTH for now.
